title: Delhi Just Banned New Petrol Two-Wheelers From 2028. No Indian City Has Gone This Far.
excerpt: India’s capital has launched its most aggressive electric vehicle policy yet — ₹15,000 crore in incentives, 30,000 new charging points, and a hard deadline that will force every new scooter buyer to go electric within two years.
body:
Starting this week, Delhi is a different city to buy a vehicle in.

The Delhi Electric Vehicles Policy 2026, notified by Lieutenant Governor Taranjit Singh Sandhu on July 1 after cabinet approval by Chief Minister Rekha Gupta, is the most aggressive EV mandate any Indian city has ever attempted. It does not merely offer carrots. It draws hard lines.

From January 1, 2027, only electric auto rickshaws and N1 category goods vehicles will be allowed new registration in the national capital. From April 1, 2028, only electric two-wheelers — no petrol, no CNG, no hybrid — will be eligible for new registration in Delhi. Existing vehicles are unaffected, but the message to manufacturers and buyers is unambiguous: the combustion engine's days in Delhi are numbered.

## ₹15,000 Crore and 30,000 Charging Points

The policy backs its mandates with serious money. The Delhi government estimates it will invest ₹15,000 crore over the next four years across incentives, charging infrastructure, and fleet electrification. The target: 95% of all new vehicle registrations in Delhi should be electric by 2027.

Buyers of electric two-wheelers will receive direct cash incentives of up to ₹30,000 in the first year, tapering to ₹10,000 by year three. Electric auto rickshaws get up to ₹50,000, and N1 electric goods carriers up to ₹1 lakh. All subsidies flow through Direct Benefit Transfer — no middlemen, no dealer markups.

Battery electric cars priced at ₹30 lakh or below receive a 100% waiver on road tax and registration fees, which typically amount to 4%–10% of a car's on-road price. For a ₹20 lakh electric sedan, that translates to savings of ₹80,000 to ₹2 lakh on day one.

The policy also earmarks over ₹1,500 crore specifically for scrappage incentives. Car owners willing to trade in BS-IV and older vehicles for an EV can receive up to ₹1 lakh — roughly $1,060 — limited to the first 100,000 applicants. More than 30,000 public EV charging points will be installed across the city during the policy period, alongside fast-charging corridors and battery-swapping stations.

## What's Excluded — and Why It Matters

In a pointed departure from some competing state policies, Delhi has excluded hybrid vehicles entirely. No incentives, no tax breaks, no registration advantages. The rationale is straightforward: in a city where vehicular pollution contributes to some of the worst air quality readings on the planet, half-measures are not enough.

The exclusion is a blow to companies like Toyota and Maruti Suzuki that have bet heavily on hybrid technology in India, and a clear win for pure-EV players. Tata Motors, Mahindra & Mahindra, Ather Energy, TVS Motor, and Bajaj Auto — all of which have committed electric two-wheeler and four-wheeler platforms — stand to gain disproportionately from a market that registers over a million new vehicles every year.

## The Air Quality Imperative

Delhi is routinely ranked among the world's most polluted cities. Winter smog, amplified by crop burning in neighbouring states, construction dust, and vehicle exhaust, has turned air quality into a public health crisis that touches every resident and every visitor.

Transport accounts for roughly 28% of Delhi's particulate matter pollution. The two-wheeler segment alone — some 6 million registered scooters and motorcycles — is the single largest contributor of vehicular NOx emissions in the city. Electrifying this segment is the fastest route to measurable improvement.

The policy's 2028 deadline for two-wheelers is ambitious but not implausible. Electric scooter prices have already fallen to within ₹10,000–₹20,000 of their petrol equivalents before subsidies. With Delhi's incentives stacked on top, an entry-level electric scooter could cost less than a comparable Honda Activa.

## The Diaspora Angle

For the millions of NRIs who fly into Delhi every year — to visit family, to invest, to consider a move back — the air quality question is not abstract. It determines whether elderly parents can walk outdoors in winter, whether children can play outside, whether a return to India is a lifestyle upgrade or a health compromise.

Delhi's EV push, if it delivers on its promises, could begin to change that calculus. The policy also signals investment opportunity. India's EV ecosystem — from lithium-ion battery manufacturing to charging infrastructure to fleet electrification — is expected to attract over $12 billion in cumulative investment by 2030. Several diaspora-backed funds have already begun allocating to Indian EV supply chains.

No state in India has provided this level of support for electric vehicle adoption, as Chief Minister Gupta noted. Whether the policy survives contact with Delhi's infrastructure reality — its grid constraints, its parking chaos, its chronic governance gaps — remains the open question. But the ambition is no longer in doubt.

*Sources: Delhi Government Gazette Notification, Reuters, YourStory, Outlook Money, Capital Market*
